item.title: Political Slop
item.content:encoded:
There are different kinds of political slop—useless nonsense that carries absolutely no useful information. But there’s one kind that really gets me. And it’s everywhere.

Here’s how it goes: make some totally inane point that would obviously never convince anyone on the other side that their position is wrong. This point might take the form of, say, pointing out that someone on the other side committed a crime. Or it might involve claiming the existence of some item of hypocrisy that is so obviously wrongheaded that its sole point is to throw sand in the other side’s eyes and to signal to your own side your commitment to the cause. Ideally it should cast the side in a negative light, but not be anything that might actually convince anyone. For example:

It’s just such outrageously silly reasoning. The main objection to kings is not that they serve for too long, after repeatedly being elected, but that they exercise too much power illegitimately. So believing that Trump is behaving in a needlessly power-grabbing way is obviously not in tension with supporting someone who has served in Congress for a bunch of years!

You wonder: did David Harris Jr. think, as he was typing this, that this was some bulletproof, unassailable point that people on the other side would have no answer to? That Bernie Sanders differs from a king in no important respects? Did he think that if someone on the other side was presented with this hypocrisy, they would throw up their hands, cry “my worldview is in fundamental tension,” and dissolve like a vampire before the light of the sun. My guess is that he did not give this comment much thought. It was simply a convenient piece of political feces to fling vaguely in the direction of the other side. It’s basically emoting—like waving a little flag and saying “boo! Democrats.”

Most claims of political hypocrisy are like this. Most of them are “you support [thing that you say is good] but this is hypocritical because you oppose [thing I think is good].” You will often hear that Republicans are hypocrites because they are only pro-life up until birth. This is a very silly claim. The Republican position isn’t that people’s lives stop mattering when they’re born. It is instead that the policies Republicans support are the best way to improve people’s lives. Perhaps they’re wrong about that, but it isn’t as if they have explicitly warring commitments that aren’t consistent. It is not hypocritical to be wrong.

And who is this supposed to convince? Who is the person who thinks that Republicans’ policies display wanton disregard for human life, but then, upon seeing that this indifference conflicts with opposition to abortion, comes to oppose Republican policies? It seems its sole purpose is to preach to the choir. To convince, in other words, those who are already convinced.

Edit 4/8: some commentators have convinced me that there are some legitimate accusations of political hypocrisy that I’d overlooked.

I suppose there is one exception to this, because there is a case where Republicans—and most people—are fairly explicitly indifferent to human life. A common political claim is that our duties extend only to other Americans. This view is in tension with being pro-life, because it implies that there aren’t any moral reasons to save the lives of most people in the world. But it’s still not hypocritical in any strict sense—there’s no contradiction—because the view of most pro-lifers is that we should prioritize American lives over others’ lives. They’re only pro-life about American children and not, say, PEPFAR recipients.

This kind of political slop is among Elon Musk’s favorite ways to communicate. Some vague and obviously question-begging claim will be made—and he’ll reply with a bullseye or by saying “interesting.”

Oftentimes the slop Elon posts will simply be an example of someone committing a crime in a way that’s supposed to favor your side (either because they’re black and Elon feels their sentence was too brief or because they committed election fraud or something). But obviously this style of argument is absurd. The world is a big place with many people committing crimes all the time; that you can find one person being sentenced too harshly or not harshly enough or committing some politically valenced crime tells nothing useful.

Certainly it seems that RFK Junior is more physically fit than Rachel Levine (assistant secretary for health under Biden). But how physically fit someone is obviously doesn’t tell you whether they’d make a good assistant secretary of health . Nobody who cheers this slop in this context would buy it in other contexts; nobody (save Clavicular) who cheers on this meme would favor an argument for Gavin Newsom over Trump on grounds that Gavin is significantly hotter.

Why does this slop go so far on the internet, especially social media? Because it doesn’t require making a sophisticated argument, it’s easy to make. It is a lot easier to post a picture of Biden’s assistant secretary of health looking less good than RFK Junior than to make serious arguments against Levine.

Social media also has a way of turning us into simplistic brutes who cheer for whatever our side does. As the algorithm rewards us for saying things that our side likes, our preferences get simpler, until we’re simply cheering for whatever our own side does, regardless of the merits. A number of people are sophisticated intellectuals outside of social media, only to become unhinged maniacs on social media.

The other reason partisan slop goes so far on the internet has to do with the phenomenon friend of the blog and alleged (though unconfirmed) happiness-inducing-cracker-feed-mumbling explained in his article The Toxoplasma Of Rage. His thesis in a nutshell was that controversy generates intrigue far better than repeating obvious truisms.

You’ve no doubt heard about PETA because of their outrageous public stunts. But it’s less likely that you’ve heard about The Humane League, even though they’ve been behind efforts to free many millions of chickens from cages. You’ve heard of Peter Singer because he says controversial things publicly; you’ve probably never heard of Derek Parfit because, though generally more careful than Singer, he was less controversial.

Less controversial pieces also come with less ability to signal. If you post on social media “I hate EVIL so much,” people will think it’s some kind of weird joke. You get no social credit for posting “when the icebox killers brutally tortured and killed people, that was really bad, and they shouldn’t have done it!” If you post political commentary on some contested topic, you get to show your side you’re one of them. The more incendiary the political commentary is—the more it would be abhorred by the other side—the greater the signaling value it has.

This is one reason why social media makes us crazy. Outrage draws clicks, so people are incentivized to be maximally uncareful and outrageous. You get what you incentivize; social media incentivizes slop and slop is what you get. You end up with, well, whatever has happened to Elon Musk’s brain. As we like more and more things that appeal to our tribal impulses, we become more tribal, and more addicted to the tribalism, until we have become like a rat on heroin—simply pushing the button each time we see some partisan hackery.

So here is my suggestion: in general, if you are posting about politics, you should try to say things that are capable, at least in principle, of convincing the other side. You should not try to vaguely shovel bad karma in the direction of your political opponents. Each time any of us do this, we are contributing to making the discourse dumber and dumber.

item.title: Burn The Stars
item.description: But if we shouldn't, God exists
item.content:encoded:
“I’m burning up a sun, just to say goodbye.”

—The 10th Doctor, one of the great scenes.

Let the sky fall
When it crumbles
We will stand tall
Face it all together

—Adele, describing the optimal post-AGI world.

In an ideal world, we would use the stars for energy to make stuff of great value. Maybe happy digital minds. Maybe happy non-digital organisms. But in any case, in the ideal future, we will burn the stars to make something better (assuming doing so is the most efficient way to convert the stars into value).1

My sense is basically everyone in the world rejects this view. Basically everyone in the world, then, is wrong.

To some, my proposal seems like a particularly alarming dystopia. Widespread transformation of the cosmos seems, to an objectionable degree, like playing God. Strangely, people don’t seem that concerned about the big chunks of space that don’t have any stars! They just think it would be concerning if we changed the distribution. You should always be wary about attributing beliefs to explicit bias, but when the belief most people have is “we should preserve the status quo, whatever it’s like,” and we know that humans have explicit biases in favor of the status quo, and the pro-status quo judgment lacks any semblance of deep theoretical support, at some point, it becomes clear that it really is just bias.

Similarly, people generally don’t think we should meddle in nature to reduce wild animal suffering. Even if this meddling really would reduce the amount of wild animal suffering in the world, they oppose it. They oppose transforming nature in pursuit of any goal—even if it’s a goal that they’re otherwise sympathetic to. In other words, even if they prefer ecosystem A to ecosystem B, they’d oppose transforming ecosystem B to A.

I find this view super implausible. And yet it’s widespread even among those who routinely criticize people for fallaciously appealing to nature for moral justification. The assumption from the outset seems to be that approximately however the universe is organized is how it ought to be organized. We shouldn’t change too much!

But such a thing would be extremely suspicious. Really, the optimal state for the world to be in is filled with the specific combination of forests, jungles, and burning gas clouds that it really is? That can’t be improved on? If so, you should certainly believe in God—for such a suspiciously fortuitous arrangement of stuff would be almost maximally unlikely given atheism.

The case against this view appeals to very simple principles. There are some things in the world that are bad and others that are good. We have reason to promote the good and to avoid the bad. Insofar as there’s lots of good that can be brought about by burning the stars, we should do it. If by default the world is massively suboptimal, we should strive to make it better!

Likewise, if bad things are present in nature, there’s strong reason to change that. And there is. The most widely agreed candidate for something that is bad is pain. Nature contains unfathomable amounts of pain. Animals by the quintillions starve, are eaten alive, suffocate, and die of thirst. Pain is bad because of how it feels. It is bad to have a headache because headaches hurt, not because the sufferer is smart. So if nature contains very large amounts of pain, there is strong reason to transform it so that it has less pain.

The best version of the view that opposes broad transformation of the world appeals to GA Cohen style conservatism. Cohen argued that good things are worth preserving. If you could replace your wife with a slightly better wife, you shouldn’t. Similarly, if you could replace the Mona Lisa with a slightly better painting, you shouldn’t do that. If things have great value, there are moral reasons not to replace them with other things, even of somewhat more value.

Thus, one might think that the natural world has value, and so it would be bad if it was replaced—even with something better. Does this vindicate opposition to major transformation of the world?

No.

Cohen-style conservatism has its limits. You should replace things of value if they could be replaced with other things of sufficiently greater value. If you could replace the Mona Lisa with peace on Earth, that would be very good. The benefits of transforming the world are very high. Unfathomable numbers of happy, wise, and in love beings could be created for each star. More welfare is at stake than all the welfare in human history so far.

And it doesn’t seem that bad for a star to be replaced. About one star dies every second in the observable universe. If stars dying was some enormous tragedy, then this would be among the worst things in the world. It’s not. Similarly, ecosystems change in huge ways all the time. If this was an enormous tragedy, then the natural drift of ecosystems would be one of the worst things in the world.

I suspect that this is just status quo bias. Imagine if stars naturally, as part of their life cycle, became fuel for supremely well-off digital minds. Would we think that was a bad thing, a tragedy to be mitigated? No, that would be great. This is importantly different from Cohen-style cases. If your child died naturally and was replaced by a better one, that would intuitively seem like a tragedy.

It also isn’t entirely clear in what sense burning the stars is a more thorough replacement than what happens naturally. Naturally, over time, stars become things that are not stars—white dwarfs, red giants, supernovas, black holes. Why is a red giant any more worthy a successor of a star than fuel for digital minds? Or than a big explosion (a supernova?) Are supernovas great tragedies?

Or take the example of nature. Why is intervention in nature supposed to be bad? I’m not talking about destroying nature—just transforming it so that it has less suffering. I’m also not discussing practical objections to this. So I won’t talk about whether there are practical ways of doing this, just whether it’s worth doing in principle.

Humans are, in a broad sense, part of nature. We evolved alongside other animals. Yet no one thinks it is bad when a new species arises naturally and changes nature. Why are we any different? If a lion can change the distribution of an ecosystem, without anything unfortunate occurring, why can’t we? Especially if the lion is doing so blindly, and we are doing so in ways that are morally optimal.

You might think this is like the argument against veganism that lions eat meat. But it’s not at all. There is a clear explanation of why one doesn’t condemn lions for eating meat but does condemn humans: lions aren’t moral agents, and they also need to eat meat to survive. It would be suspicious, however, if one thought that a lion hunting a gazelle wasn’t in any way unfortunate—didn’t result in anything morally subpar—but a human hunting a gazelle was unfortunate.

Humans interfere with nature all the time. Sometimes we rescue animals from predators or help wounded deer . That isn’t wrong. But if it’s not wrong to help a deer that’s already been wounded, why is it wrong to prevent the deer from being wounded in the first place (say, by trying to change ecosystems to minimize predator numbers and introducing birth control to manage population size)? We can even interfere for pretty trivial reasons, according to common-sense morality, like to create new industries. So if we can interfere to get a bit more wood, why can’t we do so to prevent trillions of beings from dying painfully?

Remember: behind the veil of ignorance, you would be much more likely to be a wild animal than a human. The odds you’d be born a human are lower than the odds you’ll win the lottery. Innocent beings in numbers we cannot fathom are crying out in terror and misery and pain, their blood staining the forest red. And almost everyone has the position that it’s wrong in principle to do anything about it. My crazy position is simply: if one ecosystem is much better than another, and we can transform the worse one into the better one, then we should do that, even if this involves changing how things are.

At this point, someone will say I am assuming utilitarianism. So let me say this once and for all: I am not assuming utilitarianism. I am never assuming utilitarianism. I have never, on one occasion, ever assumed as a background assumption utilitarianism. That is because utilitarianism is more controversial than the ethical claims I am arguing for. You should use more intuitive principles to prove less intuitive ones, not the other way around.

I have appealed to claims like: “there are things of value that we could do with arbitrarily large amounts of space resources” and “it is bad when animals experience intense agony in large numbers.” Neither of these claims is utilitarianism. Utilitarianism is the claim that the right action is the one that maximizes well-being. It is true that these claims contain some of the same words, and that they might look slightly similar if glimpsed on a dark night, from a distance, in a trench-coat, by someone with bad eyesight, but they are not the same.

What if you’re a theist? Should you think the world starts in an optimal state, and thus we shouldn’t transform the stars? No. First of all, on every plausible view of what is valuable in the world, the stars and trees aren’t optimal. There are other things that provide more welfare, plus more of whatever else in the world might be of intrinsic value. Second, theists already must think the world has lots of bad things: malaria, cancer, flesh-eating parasites, cognitive biases, hatred, etc. So it’s not a major addition to think that the nice bits of the natural world are still suboptimal. Theists should think that we are in part here to make things better, to help each other.

What if you adopt the person-affecting view which says that while there’s a reason to make existing people better off, there’s no reason to create people just because they’d be happy? On the PAV (as the cool kids call it) there might be no point in turning the stars into happy people, because there’s no reason to create happy people. Several things to say:

  1. The person-affecting view is false.

  2. Even if the person-affecting view is right, it’s still plausibly good to make digital minds that are successors of current organisms. It’s good that you continue in existence. But your continuing in existence, on a number of views, just involves there being some successor of you with a chain of sufficiently connected psychological states. Making there be many such successors adds still more value. And each successor must add value, otherwise whether the addition of a successor is good depends on the (non)-existence of distinct successors in distant galaxies.

  3. Even if the person-affecting view is right, and successors created don’t have value or whatever, there’s still probably something that can be done with the stars to create value. Maybe there’s a way to make existing people super well off or create great aesthetic projects by using the stars.

  4. The person-affecting view often simply denies that it’s obligatory to create happy people but grants that it’s valuable. So then burning the stars would still be of great value.

  5. This provides no argument at all against transformation of nature. In fact, if well-off organisms coming into existence isn’t fortunate, then the case for transforming nature to have less suffering is stronger, for we should worry less about lost welfare.

Thus, thinking we should burn the stars to make happy digital shrimp (or something else) isn’t just the purview of weird utilitarians: it follows on every plausible view. There are many judgments that seem bizarre before you think about them but are almost impossible to resist after careful reflection. That we should burn the stars is one of them—a truth that is surprising, yet almost trivial once you think about it.

1

In practice, I am told by my friends who know physics, probably the best way is to lift material out of stars and convert it to energy or throw stars into black holes to convert them to energy.

item.title: What To Do In Iran?
item.description: Why I don't think the policy of threatening to destroy a civilization, and then chickening out, is optimal.
item.content:encoded:
Foreign policy is dominated by half-measures. Motivated by a desire to Do Something, we often carry out feeble reprisals that achieve little more than killing a few innocent people.

Sanctions are the best example. We impose sanctions when we don’t want to start a war, but don’t want to do nothing. Sanctions rarely succeed in their aims. Broad sanctions, levied only to signal our general disapproval of the actions of a rogue state, are amazingly ineffective. They amount to little more than waging war against the civilian population of an enemy nation—a nation selected, in general, for how little they value civilian life.

Sanctions work best when we have specific policy asks in mind, but are most often imposed for basically symbolic reasons. Why, pray tell, do we still have sanctions on Cuba—what desirable policy aim is that likely to achieve? Is impoverishing and starving the Cuban people worth it for glorified finger-wagging?

Bombing often is performed similarly. In the recent case of our bombardment of Iran, it is difficult to see what we intended to achieve, and the administration has struggled to keep straight both their face and their story as they explain its motivation. Regime change? There has never in the history of the world been a case of air power enabling regime change without some pre-existing political force ready to take over. Ironically, the clearest historical example of such a “successful” air war building a political army out of nothing is the bombing of Cambodia that begot the Khmer Rouge—meaning that the one time in which a nascent political force appeared in response to bombing, it was precisely the opposite of what the bomber aimed to achieve.

So there are no examples in the history of Earth favorable to our regime change policy in Iran.

I could even see the case for America carrying out a major intervention, putting boots on the ground, and toppling the Iranian regime. I wouldn’t support it, it seems plausible that it would go the way of Iraq, but I could see the case for it. Regime changes do sometimes work—just look at Japan or Germany. But airpower alone is not enough unless there’s a serious political force on the ground ready to take over.

Opposition to airpower alone is widespread among those who have studied the subject. The most cited book on using air power to achieve foreign policy aims is Robert Pape’s Bombing to Win, representing the consensus in the field. Pape’s core thesis, from analyzing more than 30 air campaigns, is that while airpower can often degrade the military might of a regime, it isn’t good for much else. It can damage military infrastructure, making a ground invasion more effective, but on its own, it is profoundly ineffective. The usual effect of bombings is that they cause the bombarded nation to rally around their leader, making regime change more difficult.

There are some examples of airpower being useful for recent regime change: in Afghanistan, Iraq, Libya, and Kosovo. But in each of those cases, there was a real military opposition ready to take on the regime, not a disunified band of protestors. The only remotely parallel case was Kosovo, but Milosevic was initially defeated electorally—and was only ousted militarily after trying to illegally hold on to power. And even if there was one example throughout history, that would not be particularly reassuring. The Stimson Center correctly points out:

 When a government believes it is fighting for its survival, it does not capitulate. A study of thirty asymmetric interstate conflicts involving the United States from 1918 to 2003 shows that coercion most often failed when U.S. demands threated a weaker state’s survival, prompting resistance rather than capitulation. Regime change is the maximalist demand par excellence, and the Iranian government has every reason to believe its survival is at stake because Trump has said so explicitly. With everything to lose, they have no incentive to hold anything back. 

What, precisely, is the mechanism supposed to be by which this will topple the regime? America is regarded in Iran as the great Satan—just about the least popular organization on Earth. Why would bombing, while sometimes killing schoolchildren and teachers, be thought to give rise to a new political movement? Just ask: if the Trump administration got more totalitarian, so that there was a serious attempt to overthrow it, would this attempt be improved by ISIS or Iran bombing America?

What about the justification that the assault can stop Iran from getting a nuclear bomb? Preventing Iranian nuclear proliferation is a legitimate foreign policy aim, in my view. Any nation getting a nuclear weapon inches the world closer to nuclear Armageddon—especially a rogue jihadist state in the hotbed of bedlam known as the Middle East. But such a justification could at best explain the legitimacy of assaults on Iranian nuclear facilities, but not the kind of all-out bombing campaign that the U.S. launched (before chickening out the next day). The timing is also curious, occurring during talks that Omani diplomats claimed were going well (though U.S. diplomats tell a somewhat different, and less plausible, story). And if Iran was close to building a nuclear bomb, why has the Trump administration capitulated to their demands?

It is also far from clear that this policy even reduces the odds of Iran acquiring a nuclear weapon. Iran has, thus far, not pushed for nuclear armament very aggressively—aiming primarily to have the option to develop nuclear weapons if need be, rather than actually developing them. They seem to regard nuclear development as a potential bargaining chip, not something to aggressively shoot for.

Yet if the U.S. repeatedly adopts a policy of violently bombing regimes we don’t like—but only insofar as they don’t have nuclear weapons—there is a very strong incentive to build nuclear weapons. While the U.S. has aggressively enacted its will against a host of regimes, we have remained quite docile in our dealings with North Korea, because they are armed with nuclear weapons. Other nations, noticing such a pattern, are now greatly incentivized to develop nuclear weapons.

So the current policy is not working out. What should we have done? In my view, we should simply have decapitated Iranian leadership, being quite explicit that this was a response to Iran’s policies against protestors. We ought to have made clear that this was the plan in the early days of the protests, provided Iran continued to murder protestors.

A legitimate foreign policy aim is deterring extremely bad behavior. One such example of misbehavior is butchering many thousands of protestors, plausibly around 30,000, as the Iranian regime has done. Insofar as mass murder is met with no consequences, nations can mass murder with impunity. Ideally, the U.S. should send a signal: if you commit a sufficiently dramatic scale-up of human rights abuses, like killing tens of thousands of protestors, then you are signing your death warrant.

Would this have produced regime change? Likely not. Probably Khomeini would have been replaced by some other repressive, totalitarian ghoul. But the next dictator who was thinking about murdering thousands of protestors would think twice, for fear of being killed. So while decapitation is not useful for achieving regime change, or improving a regime, it can be useful for deterrence.

Of course, such a policy requires a kind of consistency and moral clarity that the present administration is incapable of. It requires that killing particularly brutal authoritarians isn’t a one-off policy, but occurs when sufficiently malevolent human rights abuses occur. I don’t expect such a policy to be adopted. But decapitations are a particularly nice tool of foreign policy, because they manage to exert quite serious deterrence on the leaders without having much negative effect domestically.

Now, Iran would probably retaliate if we decapitated their leader. But Iran is not very militarily powerful and doesn’t want an all-out war with the U.S. If we made it clear that our sole aim was to decapitate leaders who killed tens of thousands of people, probably the escalation would not go very far. Any associated cost is a small price to pay for seriously deterring unprecedented human rights abuses, on a global scale. As capably argues, decapitation doesn’t tend to escalate.

What other policies should induce decapitation? Serious human rights abuses are one example. I’d have favored the NATO intervention in Kosovo, for example (I had no opinion at the time, for I wouldn’t be born for several more years). Rogue states developing WMDs is another—and insofar as nations are reaching the point where nuclear development is imminent and a deal cannot be reached, there is a case for a stronger military intervention.

We should also expect decapitation to improve leadership quality. Insofar as we only replace leaders for carrying out particularly grotesque human rights abuses, this should shift leadership away from those who would carry out such human rights abuses. I think there was a reasonably strong case for Trump’s actions in Venezuela and Venezuela looks somewhat better today than it did at the time.

If our aim is to make the world a safer and more peaceful place, U.S. foreign policy can be a legitimate tool. Yet that requires specific and targeted deterrence, rather than the sort of broad and fickle flare-ups of the current regime. I am not optimistic that Iran will be better off as a result of the current war, and I expect its main cost to be a pox on the global economy and piles of dead Iranians.

item.title: Leading Insect Farm Took Millions In Subsidies, Then Collapsed Into A Waking Nightmare
item.description: The dark underbelly of insect farming
item.content:encoded:
I think this is an important article, so I’d really appreciate you liking, sharing, and restacking it ❤️.

A recent investigation uncovered that the leading insect farming company, Ynsect, was a horrifying disaster. While company leadership soaked up millions in subsidies with sunny rhetoric about their commercial success, the dark reality inside the farm was like nothing anyone imagined.

Investigators found filth clogging the machines, endangering workers. Larval bins would routinely break open, leading to repeated showers of larvae. Insects crawled all over the place, wholly uncontained. Airborne larval food floated haphazardly through the air, making workers sick. Birds wandered freely throughout the facility, their feces coating the machines. The whole area was a deluge of filth, feces, disease, and pollution.

The photos above show what the place looked like. In person, it was even more of a horror show. Investigators described1:

And here, in the photos and videos, you don't have the smells. In reality, it makes you dizzy. It's impossible to breathe. Even with a mask, it makes you feel sick.

The accounts from workers were even more harrowing.

There was no dust extraction, nothing at all. I started having a runny nose, itchy eyes, a scratchy throat, my nose running, my eyes burning, and difficulty breathing. Rashes on my hands, on my feet, on my knees... Everything around the joints. I had great difficulty breathing…especially in the evening when I was at home, lying down, almost sleeping outside.

Outside? Outside, in my stairwell. I couldn’t sleep lying down in my bed anymore. I held onto a railing, I thought I was going to pass out…

…

They told me they would contact occupational health, but they didn't.

That worker later relayed, “My lungs were so swollen that they were pressing against my rib cage. And that's what was preventing me from breathing.”

Ynsect is now bankrupt, having taken millions of euros in public funding and generated essentially no revenue. As Corentin Biteau, co-founder of ONEI which researches insect farming in France, notes “Ynsect’s 2023 figures were stark: €656K in revenue for €80M in losses. Maintaining insects at 25–30°C year-round, operating complex facilities, and competing with commodity feed prices proved too difficult.”

Ynsect was the industry leader. It was seen as the model of how to do insect farming right. And yet even with hundreds of millions of euros, it wasn’t remotely able to be economically viable. If the industry leader can’t avoid bankruptcy, and no one can figure out how to have a remotely viable business model, what hope is there for the insect farming industry?

What are we doing? Why do taxpayers have to fund these economically unsustainable, environmentally destructive disasters that poison workers and pollute the local environments? Why is the government taking your money and my money to fund disaster insect farms that can’t pay for themselves?

On every front, the insect farming industry is a disaster.

It’s a disaster economically. In recent years, a quarter of the 20 largest insect farms have gone bankrupt, and many of the ones that remain teeter on the edge of bankruptcy. The largest Dutch newspaper notes that investors have gotten increasingly wary about funding insect farms after their repeated economic implosions.

What is the path forward? It won’t be feeding farmed insects to people, who don’t want to eat insects and certainly won’t eat black soldier flies—the main species being farmed. The industry’s aim is to provide low-quality feed to factory farmed animals. But insect feed is much more expensive than alternative feeds, and that’s highly unlikely to change in the future. Maintaining appropriate temperatures so that the insects can grow is expensive, and the industry hasn’t found a way to cut costs.

It’s a disaster environmentally. Insects being fed to animals generate over 13 times more carbon emissions than soy-based alternatives. Nobody has been able to explain what the path forward is for the industry—even as they demand more funding from unwilling taxpayers.

When people tout insect farming as environmentally sustainable, they normally compare it to meat. And sure, if you eat a bug burger instead of a beef burger, that will be better for the environment. But no one wants to eat burgers made from bugs, so instead the insects are fed to the animals we eat. Insect farming is an industry complementary to conventional factory farming, not a competitor. If you’re concerned about the environmental footprint of factory farms, that is an argument against insect farming, not for it.

It’s a disaster on animal welfare grounds. Most animals killed each year are now farmed insects, and they’re kept in horrifying conditions without any welfare protections, even as evidence is increasingly coming in for their sentience. They’re often killed by being microwaved, suffocated, frozen, or boiled. We should be wary of boiling potentially sentient beings by the trillions, even if they’re small and don’t have many neurons. We shouldn’t do it unless there’s a good reason.

On the farms, insects are kept in overcrowded conditions where they express none of their natural behaviors. Disease is a ubiquitous feature of their lives. A report by Rethink Priorities notes “reports of larger disease outbreaks in the industry abound, including viral and fungal infections (reviewed in the paper); these diseases may be associated with significant mortality, as well as suffering related to symptoms that develop before death.”

I think we go wrong in our neglect of insects and they matter more than we naively think. It seems reasonably likely, in my view, that they can feel fairly intense pain, and the moral arguments against taking their pain seriously are not convincing. But even if you reject this view, you should always be wary about torturing trillions of beings for basically no reason. We should strive to be compassionate and not hurt animals in large number if there’s no need to do so.

You don’t have to be a bug rights activist to think that if we’re farming in hideous conditions so many bugs that most farmed animals we slaughter are now bugs, and so far no benefits have materialized at all, and there’s no story of how future benefits might materialize, and their welfare is wholly ignored even to the point where they’re microwaved to death, something very bad is going on. Scott Alexander put it well:

In the same way, even if there's only a 50-50 chance insects have moral value, or a 1% chance, still seems like you should avoid factory-farming and killing ten trillion of them, which is about how many we currently farm

…

Really any normal person should be able to take care of all their insect-harming needs without going over whatever moral budget they set for themselves - the same kind of venial sin as buying a banana even though this is probably bad for the rainforest somehow. It’s not a problem unless you’re factory-farming ten trillion insects, at which point it really starts to add up.

With conditions this dire, with feces covering and insects crawling over dilapidated machines, where workers struggle to breathe, the catastrophe isn’t contained. It spreads to the surrounding countryside, bringing novel diseases to nearby wildlife. Alarmingly, diseases on insect farms could spread. A paper by Gałęcki & Sokół found parasites in 81.33% of examined insect farms. In 30.33% of cases, parasites could infect humans. Should we risk innocent people being infected by parasites so that insect farms can make costly feed for farmed fish?

It would be one thing if insect farming provided an alternative to conventional meat. At least in that case there would be some argument for tolerating them. But in light of the fact that they are wholly without upside, tormenting trillions of insects unnecessarily, making people sick, and poisoning and polluting the surrounding landscape, they must go. It is a catastrophe and an embarrassment that so many have been duped by their bogus promises of replacing the meat industry and that taxpayers must fund their craven operations.

1

Translated from the original French.

item.title: What Continental Philosophy Defenders Cannot Explain
item.description: How we know continental philosophy is largely nonsense
item.content:encoded:
My position on continental philosophy is as simple as can be: I think much of the field, huge chunks of it, is unintelligible, gibberish, nonsense.

Continental philosophy, for those unaware, is a distinct kind of philosophy that grew out of Europe, especially France and Germany. Key thinkers in the tradition include Deleuze, Foucault, Baudrillard, Derrida, Lacan, Heidegger, etc. It is distinct from analytic philosophy in that the writing is less clear, less precise, more explicitly ideological, and centers more on answering big-picture questions than in-the-weeds technical debates.

I have no doubt that there is some good stuff somewhere in the field. It would be surprising indeed if every piece of continental writing ever written contained no useful information. But insofar as the field is, by and large, nonsense, and practitioners do not even strive for clarity, then it is in quite a dismal state.

Some people deny that continental philosophy is largely unintelligible. They claim that the core texts, once you examine them, contain a wellspring of useful and non-obvious information. Curiously, however, there is generally little agreement about what the useful and intelligible information is. I had dozens of people call me illiterate for my supposed misreadings of Butler, only for them to be wholly unable to agree on any interpretation of what Butler said!

But you might wonder: why is it that I’m so sure the field is largely nonsense? Sure, maybe I don’t understand it, but I don’t understand loads of things. I don’t understand quantum mechanics, say, but I don’t think it’s nonsense. So why this field?

My answer is in three parts.

First, because I can read. I can tell whether some passage is written in a way that’s intentionally unclear, nebulous, or obscure. It isn’t as if you can’t assess the clarity of any text provided you don’t understand exactly what’s being said. For example, here’s a paragraph in a philosophy of physics paper from an old professor of mine, writing in the analytic tradition, chosen basically at random:

With my account on the table, it is worth noting its close relationship with the picture of symmetry defended by Dewar (2015). On Dewar’s view, solutions related by symmetries should be considered equivalent, and “we can implement this [equivalence] without altering our theory, i.e., merely by making acceptable interpretational stipulations regarding the theory” (Dewar 2015: 317). For Dewar, symmetries play the same interpretive role they do on my picture: states related by symmetries are stipulated to be equivalent. But for Dewar, symmetries are not defined to be stipulated relations of equivalence. Instead he assumes they can be specified via some mathematical (formal or ontic) definition; he then urges us to stipulate that symmetries so defined relate equivalent states.

I haven’t the foggiest clue what this means. But it doesn’t strike me as unintelligible. It seems as if the author’s aim is to explain what he means, not create an impression of profundity in the mind of the reader by using big words. Contrast it with how Spivak opens Can the Subaltern Speak?

Some of the most radical criticism coming out of the West today is the result of an interested desire to conserve the subject of the West, or the West as Subject. The theory of pluralized 'subject-effects' gives an illusion of undermining subjective sovereignty while often providing a cover for this subject of knowledge. Although the history of Europe as Subject is narrativized by the law, political economy and ideology of the West, this concealed Subject pretends it has 'no geo-political determinations'. The much-publicized critique of the sovereign subject thus actually inaugurates a Subject. I will argue for this concłusion by considering a text by two great practitioners of the critique: 'Intellectuals and power: a conversation between Michel Foucault and Gilles Deleuze'.

It’s not just that I don’t know exactly what is being said (though that is certainly true). It is that the text obviously is not written for maximum clarity. Just as you can know the difference between a French speaker speaking French and a non-French speaker pretending to speak French, even if you don’t speak French, you can know the difference between clear writing and unclear writing, even if you don’t understand what either is saying.

Second, when one is clear on what the continental philosophers are saying, in nearly all cases, it ends up either trivial, unintelligible, or false. If you parse through the paper by Spivak, the thesis is basically as follows: when people in the West try to directly defer to marginalized groups, they often go wrong and import biased western assumptions that distort the contents of the demands of marginalized groups. But this is not a very interesting thesis, and does not add much beyond the obvious point that there is a process of interpretation between speaker and listener that potentially jumbles the original message.

When one cuts through the layers of jargon, the claim made by continental texts, in the end, is often just a bare assertion—or a claim that something must be true because someone else said it. Often there will be three different possible interpretations of a claim that range from the platitudinous to the preposterous (to borrow a phrase from John Searle).

Speaking of Searle, it isn’t just analytic philosophers who complain about continental gibberating. The continentals themselves admit to it. Searle recounts Foucault saying: “In France, you gotta have ten percent incomprehensible, otherwise people won’t think it’s deep–they won’t think you’re a profound thinker.” Bourdieu claimed the number was significantly higher. And there’s independent empirical evidence for it, from the fact that on multiple occasions, continental journals were hoaxed by nonsense gibberish papers which they published. Unsurprisingly, there is no comparable hoax for analytic philosophy.

So again: if continental philosophy has no problem with producing unintelligible gibberish, why do leading continental philosophers say that it does?

My third answer is that it’s not just me who finds it routinely unintelligible. This opinion is shared by many of the smartest and most philosophically equipped people I know. My friend , a Ph.D student at Princeton, recounts his experience, which is far from atypical:

In college, I took a class on continental philosophy. I read all the greats — Husserl, Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty, Levinas, Sartre, Derrida, Foucault, Levi-Strauss, Habermas, Arendt, de Beauvoir, and so on. Their writing was unintelligible to me. More importantly, it was unintelligible in a distinctive way. It was recalcitrantly unintelligible. A text is recalcitrantly unintelligible to someone just in case (i) it is unintelligible to them and (ii) those who claim to understand the text cannot make it intelligible to them.

…

I would try to understand the passage on my own and fail, sometimes even after reading the entire work containing it three or four times. Then, in class, I would express my confusion about what the passage meant. The professor would try to explain the passage to me, as would other students, but their explanations would be no less opaque to me than the passage itself. Indeed, they would almost exclusively use the very same language as the work I was struggling to interpret. As a consequence, I would make no meaningful progress toward understanding the relevant text. I eventually became skeptical that the philosophy I was reading was intelligible to anyone, including my professor.

Of the people I know who I consider best at philosophy, most share this judgment. So do Chomsky, Kit Fine, Timothy Williamson, John Searle, Michael Huemer, and Carnap. In fact, rather mysteriously, there seems to be very little correlation (and perhaps even an inverse one) between philosophical competence and appreciation of continental philosophy. While many of the most eminent and brilliant philosophers in the world can’t make heads or tails of Heidegger, a sizeable portion of undergraduates claim to be able to. Maybe you deny that undergraduates can understand continental texts, but if so, then presumably you shouldn’t favor teaching them to undergraduates?

This is quite an odd situation. Notice: there aren’t parallels in other difficult fields. It isn’t as if half of working mathematicians think that Terence Tao is speaking gibberish, but undergraduates who approach the work with no formal training believe it to be a work of genius. Indeed, the personality trait that seems to correlate most strongly with appreciation of continental philosophy is excessive charity—a willingness to, when confronted with a baffling and implausible claim, say “well surely he meant,” before subbing in some watered-down claim of your own that sort of rhymes with the original claim.

Here is my diagnosis of the phenomenon. Continental philosophers generally do not have thoughts that are very clear and precise. When they write, concrete descriptions melt away into flurries of abstractions and meta claims that aren’t sharp enough to be either true or false. Because the writing is, by and large, really bad, most people give up and do not try to interpret them.

Those who do find something of use in them do so for one of two reasons. The first is that they are drawn in by the pseudo-profundity. There is a common assumption that if a writing is complex, it must be profound—there must be some deep wisdom to squeeze out of it. Thus, those aesthetically drawn to this kind of performance try to extract something deep. And because the writing is so nebulous, so imprecise, anyone attributing a straightforward error to a writer of continental philosophy can always be accused of misunderstanding.

The second kind of people who are drawn to this writing are those who are excessively charitable. The excessively charitable are convinced at the outset that any item of writing must have something useful in it. Given the malleability of continental text, they have an easy time contorting the meaning into something true—given their psychological disposition towards finding good in unclear texts. Continental philosophy serves as a kind of Rorschach test where one can find almost anything in it. If you are stubbornly committed to thinking the author must be on to something, then you will inevitably be able to find some claim that isn’t totally crazy in a continental text.

Notice that this theory explains every one of the puzzling facts about continental writing. Because continental philosophy lacks any highly precise meaning, it is no surprise that its practitioners frequently admit to being intentionally obscure. Similarly, this theory predicts that when continental texts are translated to be precise and plain, they will end up looking trivial or unintelligible. Beneath the deluge of words, nothing specific is being said.

And it explains why people’s tendency to find continental philosophy useful correlates much more with psychological dispositions than with philosophical competence. Insofar as getting meaning from continental texts is a process that demands generation from the reader—and not merely interpretation, that it is a sort of choose-your-own-adventure game—it is no surprise that those excessively prone to charity will find the texts profound, and some of the most brilliant people on Earth will find them vacuous.

I should note, this is not just a property of continental philosophical writing. It is a property of bad writing in general, that it will remain lofty and nebulous—so that you get a vague sense of what is being argued, rather than any precise meaning. Nearly any utterance will have some degree of imprecision. But though continental philosophy is not unique in possessing ambiguity and imprecision, it is in a league all its own regarding the degree of imprecision. Comparing the imprecision of continental texts to analytic texts is like comparing the Pacific Ocean to a swimming pool.

In fact, I think a similar thing is often true of history of philosophy. Most philosophers writing in the deep past had thoughts that were fairly muddled, underdetermined between a number of distinct interpretations. For this reason, if a reader is steadfastly convinced at the outset that they must have something useful to say, they can always find some item of apparent wisdom. It is suspicious that, say, Kant scholars rarely attribute to him a clear unambiguous error, even though non-Kant scholars think he’s making huge blunders all the time. Other writers, like Curtis Yarvin, generate similar tendencies in their defenders—because Yarvin’s writing is imprecise, his defenders claim in it far more cleverness than is actually present (which is to say, any non-zero level of cleverness).

Of course, I wouldn’t suggest that all continental philosophy has the same degree of imprecision. My sense is that though Foucault is often obscure and imprecise, one frequently finds claims in his writing that are non-trivial, and some of them might even be true. Some continental philosophy has useful nuggets buried beneath the clouds of abstraction.

Now, I could imagine some proponents of continental philosophy simply biting the bullet. “Sure, our writing lacks precise meaning to a high degree—what’s wrong with that?” Well, what is wrong with that is that if one wants to analyze some set of ideas, they must know what the ideas are. Insofar as the ideas shapeshift into whatever form avoids your objections, so that two interpreters can’t agree on what’s being said, meaningful scrutiny is impossible. Otherwise, the speakers may as well be speaking a foreign language, where you can make out a few words and get a vague sense of what is being said, but cannot precisely analyze the arguments in question.

When writing remains nebulous, you can’t have any assurance that it’s going right. If a text has 15 different potential meanings, and merely communicates a vague and indeterminate impression across them, then insofar as it has convinced you, it has done so for non-rational reasons. Furthermore, if reasoning remains cloudy and nebulous, it is very easy for errors to seep in. The way analytic philosophy improves thinking is by forcing claims to be precise and subjecting them to rigor. Insofar as claims remain formless and are never subject to rigor, there’s little hope for progress.

What is the explanation favorable to continental philosophy of why so many philosophically equipped people can’t make heads or tails out of texts that undergraduates can routinely supposedly understand? Is there some unique pathology, faced by half the world’s most brilliant people, that leaves them wholly unable to comprehend plain and perspicuous prose, yet curiously lacking among droves of pretentious high-school students?

Why do leading experts in philosophy claim with such frequency that the continentals are engaged in pseudophilosophy and charlatanism? On such a picture, something deeply bizarre is going on without any parallel in all the rest of human life. The other story—that people have been drawn in by charlatans using big words to feign profundity—is a fairly ubiquitous feature of human life, and a much better explanation of every single one of continental philosophy’s puzzling features.

item.title: A Lot Of Arguments Against Immigration Are Arguments For Anti-Natalism
item.content:encoded:
There are two ways to deal with an argument. One is to show how it goes wrong. Another is to show that it’s wrong, without showing how it’s wrong—often by illustrating that it proves too much. For example, you might show that the argument that it’s okay to eat meat because lions do it goes wrong, because if sound, it would imply that it was permissible to eat human children.

The arguments against immigration can be dealt with either way. When one investigates the factual premises, they generally don’t hold up. But many of them have another, deeper problem: if they were sound, they’d be fully general arguments against population increases.

Here are some things that people say about why they oppose immigration.

“Immigrants take jobs.” But so do new people brought into the world. If the population doubled, there’d be twice as many people taking jobs. Why would that not be catastrophic?

“Immigrants change culture.” But so does population turnover. That is, in fact, the primary engine of cultural generation. We’d have a very different culture if Gen-Z had never existed. Of course, there might be specific reasons to think the effects of immigration on culture are uniquely bad. But absent that, just noting that immigrants make a big difference to the fabric of America isn’t sufficient to show it’s a bad idea.

“Immigrants commit crimes.” But so, of course, do young people. In fact, while immigrants commit crimes at lower rates than others, young people commit crimes at significantly higher rates. If everyone stopped having kids, crime rates would go down, while if all immigration was banned, crime rates would go up.

“Immigrants use public services.” Again, so do new people who were born.

Now, you could simply grant that these are downsides of new generations, but think that they are outweighed by the upsides. So, for example, you’d think it’s a bad thing that new generations change culture, but this is outweighed by the upsides of there being new people in the world. But this has two issues.

First, this isn’t what we’re inclined to think. We don’t think that population increases are bad on grounds they increase crime. Insofar as they lower the crime rate, so that the odds of existing people being victimized go down, this seems like an upside all-things-considered instead of a downside. Similarly, we think it’s good that future generations change the culture. It would be horrifying if we permanently locked in the culture of the 1920s.

Second, the person pushing this line must then explain the difference between immigration and having children in these regards. Why is it that the upsides of children entering the country and disrupting culture outweigh the downsides, but the downsides of immigrants entering the country and disrupting culture outweigh the upsides? The benefits seem fairly symmetrical. And if anything, standard ethical assumptions imply that we should put more weight on those who exist than those who merely will exist in the future. I don’t buy this ethical assumption, but I also don’t buy the one opposed to immigration.

Now you might object: to prevent child-rearing, we’d have to exercise very harmful coercion. So it’s totally different from immigration restrictions. But this doesn’t defuse the challenge.

  1. Immigration restrictions also require employing harmful coercion. It involves state power being used to make it illegal for people to enter whole countries, where their incomes might quintuple and they might be freed from the yoke of tyranny, gang violence, and oppression.

  2. At most, this could explain why there’s an asymmetry between immigration restrictions and restrictions on having children. But the view most people have isn’t just that having kids shouldn’t be illegal, but that it’s actively fortunate when new kids are brought into the world. So this explanation won’t justify the belief that being brought into the world is good, but immigrants being brought into a country is bad.

Now, I don’t mean to suggest that this rebuts every single argument against immigration. If your concerns about immigration are brain-drain related or if you have highly specific cultural concerns—having to do with degrading institutions, rather than just generic cultural turnover—then this objection won’t help much. But at least it illustrates that the standard objections to immigration are too quick. Just noting that immigrants commit crimes sometimes does nothing to settle the question of whether immigration is fortunate.

To oppose immigration sensibly, you will need some specific complaint about immigrants that doesn’t apply to people in general. You will need some explanation of a problem unique to immigrants, that doesn’t arise generally for new people being brought into the world.

But probably that won’t be enough. For example, suppose that your concern was that immigrants tend to be net fiscal drains and commit crimes at higher rates than others. Neither of those is true, but putting aside that small problem, that still doesn’t seem sufficient to justify opposition to immigration. Because there are some demographics of people that commit crimes at higher rates and are fiscal drains on average. Nonetheless, we don’t think their coming into existence is unfortunate. We don’t think every demographic that on average takes more money than it brings in and commits crimes at higher rates should not exist.

So maybe immigration restrictionists just should be anti-natalists. Weird that the views are inversely correlated!

item.title: Some Interesting Things I’ve Read Recently
item.description: On funerals keeping Africa poor, miracles, effective altruism, cancer, AI preparedness, telescopic altruism, data centers, Sam Bankman Fried, Dominion, fallacies, and love, plus a personal update
item.content:encoded:
First a personal update: I’m in Oxford working for Forethought for the next several months, after which I’ll begin a philosophy Ph.D at Princeton. Let me know if you are in either location and would like to meet up! Okay, onto the interesting things I’ve read.

I’ve said it before and I’ll say it again— has one of the best blogs on substack. In a recent piece titled How funerals keep Africa poor, Oks notes the bewildering fact that in many African countries, average expenditure on a single funeral is several times the annual income in the country. He explains that this is part of a broader cultural feature that impedes economic growth, whereby people are expected to make costly signals of kinship ingroup loyalty, preventing individuals from getting ahead. Thoughtful explanation of a deeply bizarre phenomenon. Particularly mind-blowing paragraph:

Out of 325 families that declined into poverty in western Kenya over a period of 25 years, 63 percent cited “heavy expenses related to funerals” as a major cause. And this doesn’t seem to be a new thing. As early as 1853, a visitor to coastal West Africa noted that “even the poorest will pawn and enslave themselves to obtain the means of burying a relation decently, according to the ideas of country.”

(edit: see here for claims that this phenomenon isn’t as widespread as Oks says).

His other articles are great too! Especially popular has been Why ATMs didn’t kill bank teller jobs, but the iPhone did. I also met Oks briefly and can attest that he’s a pretty cool guy!

How effective is effective altruism, you might wonder. in his recent piece on EA successes answers: staggeringly effective. Since its inception, EA has saved around 300,000 lives, spared 100 million hens from a cage per year, and contributed positively to pandemic preparedness and mitigation of AI risks.

300,000 lives is about the population of Oxford and Cambridge combined, meaning that the number of lives EA has saved directly is equivalent to preventing a nuclear bomb from wiping both Oxford and Cambridge off the map. Pretty extraordinary for a small movement! And best of all, EA is rapidly growing! You’d think that EA critics would find that fact more worth mentioning than whatever random things that sound bad out of context Nick Beckstead said in his Ph.D thesis 12 years ago.

The link also has Will’s complete appearance on the podcast. Sam posed good questions, but I felt like Will extremely convincingly dispatched every objection Sam raised.

Ben Sasse was always one of my favorite senators from the other side of the aisle. He always seemed clearly to be a man of both principle and integrity. Tragically, he is dying of pancreatic cancer. His appearance on Ross Douthat’s podcast is an excellent example of how one should live on the brink of death—and he confronts his impending demise with humor, decency, and courage.

The organization I work for, Forethought, is constantly churning out hugely important pieces of research. In a recent one, and provide extremely specific and concrete projects for making a world of advanced AI go better. I would highly encourage some people to work on these projects which could make the difference between a post-AGI world that goes well and one that goes badly. The top five proposals:

AI character evaluation. Start an independent org to evaluate and stress-test AI character traits (epistemic integrity, prosociality, appropriate refusals), hold developers accountable against their own model specs / constitutions, and suggest and incentivise improvements to the specs.

Automated macrostrategy. Create evaluations and benchmarks, collect human-generated training data, and build scaffolds to improve AI competence at big-picture strategic and philosophical reasoning.

AI security assessment. Start an independent org that evaluates AI models for sabotage and backdoors, and makes recommendations about AI constitutions.

Enabling deals. Start an independent organisation to broker deals with potentially misaligned AI models in order to incentivise early schemers to disclose misalignment and cooperate with alignment efforts.

AI for improving collective epistemics. E.g. build an AI chief of staff that helps users act in line with the better angels of their nature.

See more of Forethought’s research here.

Elizabeth Barrett Browning’s poem How Do I Love Thee is very good! It manages to capture perfectly the kind of deep love involved in caring about another person as you do yourself, where they are like a part of you, distinguished from the immediate rush of affection that accompanies the beginning of romantic relationships. As C.S. Lewis says “Love is not affectionate feeling, but a steady wish for the loved person’s ultimate good as far as it can be obtained.”1 Insofar as your care for another person extends only as far as the fuzzy feelings they engender in you, your love is of the feeling and not of them.

writes very clever, well-written, and careful pieces. In a recent one, he gets to the bottom of the “are claims evidence?” controversy. His view, that claims are evidence, and their evidential status works just the same way as every other item of evidence, is clearly right. Silas’s April fool’s day post was also by far the funniest thing I read on April fools.

I’ve mentioned before that is almost superhumanly persuasive in person. In his online debates, he’s generally pretty restrained, and sticks to dryly recounting the facts rather than doing much editorializing. Well, in his recent interview with , Ethan turned the persuasiveness dial up to 11—and you can see clearly why he’s a force to be reckoned with in arguments. I don’t think the case for Fatima being miraculous is very good, but man it sounds good when he presents it.

Speaking of Ethan, someone also cleaned up the audio for his debate about Lanciano with Stacy Trasancos, so that it’s listenable now. This Friday, he’ll also be debating with about whether apparently Catholic miracles are demonic deceptions (for once on Catholic miracles, I agree with Ethan—I don’t think Fatima was a demonic deception!)

In his crusade to defend Catholicism, Ethan wrote a piece arguing that the Lanciano relic was miraculous. Maxime Georgel wrote a reply, Ethan replied to that, and now Georgel has replied to his reply. The last reply is in French, but you can easily translate it.

Ethan also has a piece about Padre Pio that I haven’t yet seen a good response to. Someone should write up a comprehensive reply (there’s one reply but it’s very far from comprehensive, and the author mostly ignored Ethan’s objections)! It also seems like explaining apparent miracles is a good way to grow your blog.

(I thought this video was pretty good but not comprehensive).

Speaking of Fatima, uncovers a Buddhist analogue of Fatima. Arthur’s substack is also cool for investigating a lot of apparent miracles and things that obviously aren’t miracles but bear suspicious resemblances to miracles. also comments on the Buddhist miracle.

Speaking of Scott, here he demolishes the concept of telescopic altruism. Lots of people claim that caring about people on the other side of the world is a smoke-screen for neglecting those nearby—that supposedly compassionate liberals use sanctimonious rhetoric about foreigners to justify hating their neighbors and their countrymen. Scott explains why this charge doesn’t hold up—the whole thing is worth reading, but here’s a representative quote:

“Telescopic altruism” is a supposed tendency for some people to ignore those close to them in favor of those further away. Like its cousin “virtue signaling”, it usually gets used to own the libs. Some lib cares about people in Gaza - why? Shouldn’t she be thinking about her friends and neighbors instead? The only possible explanation is that she’s an evil person who hates everyone around her, but manages to feel superior to decent people by pretending to “care” about foreigners who she’ll never meet.

This collapses upon five seconds’ thought. Okay, so the lib is angry about the Israeli military killing 50,000 people in Gaza. Do you think she would be angry if the Israeli military killed 50,000 of her neighbors? Probably yes? Then what’s the problem?

“But vegetarians care about animals more than humans!” Okay, yeah, they sure do get mad about a billion pigs kept for their entire lives in cages too small to turn around in, then murdered and eaten. Do you think they’d care if a billion of their closest friends were kept for their entire lives in cages too small to turn around in, then murdered and eaten? I dunno, seems bad.

See also Being John Rawls from Scott which is one of the best essays I’ve ever read.

Recently, a ridiculous clown paper made the case that data centers were heating the surrounding area, which was then uncritically reported on by the media. takes it apart, noting that the methodology relied on comparing the temperature of the concrete the data center was made from to the surrounding cooler vegetation. See also his brilliant essay Animal Suffering Isn’t Pretend.

Chalmers solves the two envelopes problem.

explains, using fission cases, why even person-affecting views will imply some analogue of the repugnant conclusion. His papers are, without exception, very high quality, and his blog is good too!

explains why the world should stop talking so much about Sam Bankman Fried.

If you spend more than five seconds in the bay area, someone will inevitably ask you what your timelines are—when you think artificial general intelligence will be developed. But Toby Ord rightly points out, you should have uncertainty about timelines. Rather than banking on either short or long timelines, you should have broad timelines, and favor actions that are good whether AI comes soon or later.

reviews Dominion, a book by George W. Bush speechwriter Matthew Scully, making the case that our treatment of animals is an abomination. Scully’s book is excellent and so is the review—its end is particularly haunting.

has another great blog that I only started following recently. His article criticizing the concept of logical fallacies excellently distilled quite an important point. I also appreciated his review of Chomsky vs. Foucault. And over on Twitter, he posted a devastating and hilarious review of Anti-Oedipus.

Our World In Data concisely distills the evidence for human-driven megafauna extinction (see also my article on the subject). Since publishing my article, Paul Shapiro on Twitter gave me another strong argument for megafauna extinction being driven by human hunting: all the extinct species were land animals. This makes sense on the hunting hypothesis since humans mostly hunted land creatures. But if it was caused by warming, it should target the sea too. Especially because global warming has disproportionately harmed sea creatures.

Reasonable candidate for the best video on YouTube. Another good one.

Jack Symes recently appeared on Jubilee to debate veganism with 20 people. He humanely slaughtered them, showing a masterclass performance. The comments are unanimously on his side, even from meat eaters.

Insect farming is presently an economically non-viable dumpsterfire. But you might wonder: will it become viable in the future? A paper analyzed this question and concluded the answer is no—the problems just run too deep and are inherent to the industry. See also Kenny Torella’s article about the abject failure of insect farming.

Spencer Case has a great podcast. In a recent highly-informative episode, he brought on four philosophers to debate the Iran war. I thought the anti-war side made a better case.

Lots of people are pessimistic about philosophy. But in his book, freely available online, Herman Capellan argues convincingly that philosophy is great, among other things because it has uncovered the right answer to most of the deep questions. Of course, there’s not universal agreement on what the right answer is, but mapping out the terrain and identifying the true view is a pretty huge accomplishment.

wrote a nice post on Valentine’s day about love. One of the more heart-warming things I’ve read. He also has a nice piece destroying Randian objectivism.

Nabokov’s Pale Fire is really good. It starts with a lengthy poem, and then things get a bit strange. I particularly loved this bit:

Retake the falling snow: each drifting flake
Shapeless and slow, unsteady and opaque,
A dull dark white against the day’s pale white
And abstract larches in the neutral light.

1

That definition cannot be quite right. I have a steady wish for the welfare of shrimp, say, but I do not love them. To love someone, you must have not merely a steady wish for their ultimate good, so that you care for it somewhere like your own ultimate good, but also a desire for some kind of unity with them. This unity takes different shapes—the kind of love you might have for a friend would lead you to want to spend time with them, the kind of love had for a lover comes with its own desired forms of unity that would be scandalous if directed at a family member. But in each case, to love someone requires that you want to maintain some kind of relationship with them all else equal.

item.title: Before Making Sweeping Claims About Epistemology, You Should Think About Whether They Imply Something Obviously Absurd
item.description: And whether, for example, they'd vaporize all scientific knowledge
item.content:encoded:
One of the bad habits of people arguing against the existence of God is to make epistemological claims which, if applied consistently, would imply that no one knows anything. It’s especially funny when a new atheist accidentally endorses some epistemological principle that implies there’s no evidence for evolution.

For example, proponents of the fine-tuning argument will often say that the odds of the constants being in the narrow range that gives rise to life are very low. A common reply is “no, the odds are 100%, because the world is finely-tuned.” But think about applying this to any other probabilistic setting. Imagine we’re playing poker, and I get ten royal flushes in a row. It is reasonable to say that the odds of my getting such an extraordinary stream of luck are low, even though we now know that I have gotten it. For on the bare assumption that I am playing fairly, the probability is low.

A major respect in which philosophers think more clearly than non-philosophers is that when someone makes a big sweeping claim, philosophers think about whether it has some obvious counterexample.

A philosopher friend of mine relays a story where he was talking with a historian who smugly preened “as historians, we recognize that there are no such things as eternal truths.” “Is that an eternal truth?” my friend asked. He was met with stunned silence. It was as if the historian had never given the question any thought. Probably what had happened was that the historian had said this one time, it had sounded cool, and so he’d just repeated it, without thinking through whether it had any obvious counterexamples.

One common new atheist claim was that you first have to demonstrate that something is possible before adducing evidence for it. But what does that mean? How did historians demonstrate that Julius Caesar was possible before proving that he existed? How did physicists demonstrate that the bending of time or the existence of dark matter was possible before getting evidence for it?

People also often claim that for a belief to be justified, it must be falsifiable. There must, in other words, be some way that it could be disconfirmed—some experiment that could be run which could prove it false. But that view is self-defeating. How, pray tell, would one falsify that very claim? Similarly, how would one falsify the belief that everything is identical to itself or that it is possible for the world to be larger than however large it in fact is? How would one falsify the belief that there aren’t any invisible wholly undetectable pixies on the moon?

Or often cultural relativists will claim that there’s no such thing as objective morality because people disagree about it. Before making such a claim, you should stop to think: are there things that are objective but that people disagree about? Answer: yes, obviously. The roundness of the Earth, to take one notable example. So mere disagreement doesn’t suffice to prove subjectivity.

Another class of arguments that proves too much is basically everything normal people say when explaining why they’re not vegan. For example, people often justify their non-veganism by noting that lions eat meat. But ask: are there things lions do sometimes that you should not (eating human children, for instance)? If so, then you should not use lions to vindicate the morality of some behavior.

Or people will explain that it’s okay to eat meat because it’s natural. But a lot of things are natural and bad—malaria, for instance, and flesh-eating parasites, and dying at the age of 35. Or people will argue it’s alright to eat meat because we’ve been doing it since ancient times. But this is also an argument for war, rape, and slavery, so it proves too much.

When explaining why they don’t think Jesus rose from the dead, atheists will often repeat the slogan “claims aren’t evidence.” But claims very often are evidence. Evidence is anything that renders a hypothesis more likely—when someone claims something, that renders it a bit more likely. No matter how unlikely you think it is that Jesus rose from the dead, you should no doubt think it would have been more unlikely if nobody ever claimed to have seen him posthumously. The odds Jesus rose from the dead are higher than the odds, say, Muhammed did. Most of our evidence for historical claims takes the form of testimony.

Of course, there’s a further question of whether there’s enough evidence to make it reasonable to think Jesus rose. I don’t think there is. But to dismiss the relevant testimony as not evidence at all is an error. Evidence is pretty easy to come by—you just need to find any fact that’s likelier if some hypothesis is true than if it’s false.

Or people often claim that in order to have evidence, you need to make some prediction about the future that comes true. But this isn’t how most of the evidence for evolution came in. Similarly, because historians never make predictions, it would mean we had no evidence for any historical claim.

I once heard Ricky Gervais explain that the thing that differentiates science from religion, with respect to the evidence in their favor, is that if science died out, we could rediscover it. In contrast, if religion died out, we couldn’t. The point, I guess, was supposed to be that this put science on firmer epistemological footing than religion because it is repeatable—and meant that religion was a tissue of unproven assumptions. This was his explanation of why he was an atheist.

But notice: this is also an argument against history. If we destroyed all the documents attesting to the existence of Julius Caesar, future people could not work out, by reason alone, that he existed. Similarly, it is an argument for me being unable to know with confidence what I had for lunch today, for if all the information about this died off, humanity could not rediscover it from first principles.

I would like to boldly submit, then, that if you are going to make some sweeping claim about how evidence works, you should take a few minutes, at some point in your life, to consider if it is true. Such would avoid a number of embarrassing errors. When repeating some quip about how evidence works, the primary thing you should consider is not whether it sounded cool when Christopher Hitchens said it, but whether it is actually correct.

item.title: Are The Fatima Children Unprecedented?
item.description: Analyzing in detail some underdiscussed Fatima arguments
item.content:encoded:
1 Think of the children?
